actions.title: Follow official warnings
actions.detail: Keep a radio or phone charged. Listen for official warnings and instructions from local authorities and volunteers.

actions.title: Agree on a meeting point
actions.detail: Choose a place where your family will meet if you get separated, and make sure every member knows it.

actions.title: Protect your documents
actions.detail: Put ID cards, land papers, and medical records in a waterproof plastic bag in your go-bag. You may need ID to receive relief.

actions.title: Label your children
actions.detail: Write your name and phone number on a paper in each child's pocket, or on their arm with a pen, in case you are separated.

actions.title: Pack at least 7 days of medicine
actions.detail: Keep medicines and prescriptions in your go-bag. Ask your clinic for an extra supply when a warning is issued.

actions.title: Plan for power-dependent medical equipment
actions.detail: Tell your local health worker and disaster committee now that someone depends on powered equipment. Go early to a shelter with power or a hospital.

actions.title: Arrange help to move
actions.detail: Ask a neighbour, volunteer or relative now to help move family members who cannot walk far. Agree who will come and when.

actions.title: Tell someone your plan
actions.detail: You live alone. Share your plan and shelter with a neighbour or relative and agree to check on each other.

actions.title: Know where you could give birth
actions.detail: Find the nearest health facility that can help with delivery and keep your antenatal card in your go-bag. Tell shelter staff you are pregnant.

actions.title: Pack for your baby
actions.detail: Breastfeeding is safest during disasters. If you use formula, pack ready-to-use formula, clean bottles and safe water.

actions.title: Bring pets if you can
actions.detail: Take pets on a leash or in a carrier. Not all shelters accept animals — check the shelter features in this app.

actions.title: Register for relief
actions.detail: Register your household with local officials or at the shelter so you are included in relief lists. See 'Programs for you' below.

actions.title: Drink only safe water
actions.detail: Boil water, use purification tablets, or drink bottled water. Diarrhoea and cholera spread quickly after disasters.

actions.title: Protect young children from dirty water
actions.detail: Young children get sick fastest. Use oral rehydration salts (ORS) at the first sign of diarrhoea and seek care.

actions.title: Let family know you are safe
actions.detail: Send a short message to your emergency contacts. Keep calls short so networks stay open for rescue.

actions.title: Move livestock to high ground early
actions.detail: Move animals to a raised killa or shelter with livestock space before the storm. Do not go back for animals once the wind is strong.

actions.title: Secure your house
actions.detail: Tie down the roof with rope, close and board windows, and bring loose items inside. Store drinking water in clean containers.

actions.title: Your house is not safe in a cyclone
actions.detail: Mud, tin, wood houses and tents can collapse or blow away. Go to a cyclone shelter or strong concrete building as soon as evacuation is announced.

actions.title: Storm surge: move inland or up
actions.detail: Most cyclone deaths are from storm surge (sea water flooding). Leave low coastal land early — do not wait for the wind.

actions.title: Leave early
actions.detail: Your family will need more time to move. Start for the shelter at the first evacuation warning, not the last.

actions.title: Stay inside until it is officially over
actions.detail: Stay away from windows. The calm 'eye' of the storm is not the end — strong winds will come back from the other direction.

actions.title: Avoid fallen power lines and damaged buildings
actions.detail: Do not touch wires or enter damaged buildings. Report hazards to authorities.

actions.title: Raise valuables and food
actions.detail: Put food, seeds, documents and valuables on a high shelf or platform. Store clean drinking water.

actions.title: Watch the river level
actions.detail: You live near a river. Sign up for flood warning SMS and watch water levels — floods can rise quickly at night.

actions.title: Move animals before water rises
actions.detail: Take livestock to embankments, raised platforms or shelters with livestock space early.

actions.title: Upper floors are a last resort
actions.detail: Your house has more than one floor. If you cannot leave, move to the highest floor — but do not go into a closed attic where you could be trapped.

actions.title: Leave before water enters your home
actions.detail: Your home has one floor, so there is nowhere higher to go. Go to the nearest flood shelter or high ground at the first warning.

actions.title: Never walk or drive through flood water
actions.detail: 15 cm of moving water can knock you down; 60 cm can carry away a car. Water may hide holes and electric wires.

actions.title: Do not drive into water
actions.detail: Turn around if a road is flooded. Most flood drownings happen in vehicles.

actions.title: Watch for snakes and sharp debris
actions.detail: Wear shoes, use a stick when walking through debris, and check the house before going back in.

actions.title: Practise Drop, Cover, Hold On
actions.detail: Drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck under a strong table, and hold on until shaking stops. Practise with your family.

actions.title: Fix heavy items
actions.detail: Tie or bolt tall furniture, water tanks and gas cylinders to the wall. Do not keep heavy items above beds.

actions.title: Your house may not resist strong shaking
actions.detail: Mud and unreinforced brick houses are the most dangerous in earthquakes. Ask local engineers or NGOs about retrofitting, and identify the safest spot near a strong exit.

actions.title: If you use a wheelchair: Lock, Cover, Hold On
actions.detail: Lock your wheels, bend forward and cover your head and neck with your arms or a pillow until the shaking stops.

actions.title: Do not run outside while shaking
actions.detail: Most injuries happen from falling objects while people run. Stay where you are, Drop, Cover and Hold On. If outside, move away from buildings, walls and wires.

actions.title: Go to an open space
actions.detail: After shaking stops, leave carefully and go to an open space away from buildings. Expect aftershocks.

actions.title: Do not sleep inside a damaged house
actions.detail: Cracked walls can collapse in aftershocks. Stay in an open space or official camp until an engineer checks your house.

actions.title: Watch for landslides
actions.detail: Earthquakes loosen slopes. Stay away from steep hillsides and river banks for several days.

actions.title: Strong shaking near the sea? Go to high ground
actions.detail: A long or strong earthquake near the coast can cause a tsunami. Walk to high ground immediately — do not wait for a warning.

actions.title: Know the warning signs
actions.detail: New cracks in the ground or walls, tilting trees or poles, muddy water in streams, or rumbling sounds mean a landslide may be coming.

actions.title: Leave slopes during heavy rain
actions.detail: Your home is on or below a slope. During heavy or long rain, move to a safer place away from the slope and river channels, especially at night.

actions.title: Move sideways, not downhill
actions.detail: If you see or hear a landslide, move quickly out of its path to the side. Do not try to outrun it downhill.

actions.title: Stay away from the slide area
actions.detail: More slides can follow. Do not return until officials say it is safe. Report trapped people to rescuers instead of digging alone.

actions.title: Know the natural warning signs
actions.detail: A strong earthquake, the sea suddenly pulling back, or a loud roar from the ocean means a tsunami may be coming. Go to high ground immediately.

actions.title: Know your route to high ground
actions.detail: Find a place at least 10 m above sea level or 2 km inland that you can reach on foot in 15 minutes.

actions.title: Walk to high ground now
actions.detail: Go on foot — roads jam quickly. If you cannot reach high ground, go to the upper floor of a strong concrete building.

actions.title: Carry those who cannot run
actions.detail: There may be only minutes. Carry small children and help elderly or disabled family members immediately; leave belongings behind.

actions.title: Stay on high ground for hours
actions.detail: Tsunamis come in several waves and the first is often not the largest. Wait for an official all-clear.

kit.label: Drinking water (3 litres per person per day, for 3 days)
Dry food that does not need cooking (chira, muri, biscuits, dates, canned food)
Torch / flashlight and spare batteries
Battery radio or charged phone with power bank
ID cards and important papers in a waterproof bag
First aid kit, soap, ORS sachets, water purification tablets
Some cash in small notes
Whistle to call for help
Change of clothes, plastic sheet, rope
7+ days of medicines and copies of prescriptions
Nappies/cloths, baby food or formula, clean bottle, baby blanket
Small toy or book for each child, name/phone note in pocket
Spare glasses, walking stick, hearing aid batteries
Wheelchair repair kit, cushion, any mobility aids
Antenatal card, clean delivery kit, sanitary pads
Backup batteries for medical devices and a list of device settings
Leash or carrier, food and water for pets
Fodder, rope, and tags to identify your animals
Dust masks and sturdy shoes
Something that floats (empty jerrycan, banana-trunk raft) and rope
